patient_information: A 7-year-old girl who lives in the Peruvian capital, Lima, is otherwise healthy.
chief_complaint: A chronic skin lesion on her nose, present for 4 months.
history_of_present_illness: The lesion appeared 4 months ago as a small nodule and slowly turned into an ulcer. It is a bit itchy but not painful. There is no history of trauma.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient lives in the Peruvian capital, Lima. Six months ago, she travelled to a valley on the western slopes of the Andes. Cutaneous leishmaniasis is common in endemic areas and specifically in the valley the patient had traveled to.
physical_exam: The lesion is a localized ulcer on the nose (Fig. 2.1). The borders of the ulcer are indurated and there is a plaque-like infiltration of the surrounding skin. The whole lesion is about 2 cm in diameter. There are no palpable lymph nodes. The rest of the physical examination is normal. The scab was removed revealing an ulcer with cobblestone-patterned bottom and raised edges, typical of cutaneous leishmaniasis.
labs_and_diagnostics: Microscopic examination of a sample obtained by scraping was negative. The leishmanin skin test was positive. PCR was also positive; and the infecting species was identified as Leishmania (Viannia) peruviana.
differential_diagnosis: Infectious diseases considered included cutaneous leishmaniasis, sporotrichosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, and infection by Balamuthia mandrillaris. Common bacterial infections of the skin were considered less likely given the chronic nature. Cutaneous anthrax and tularaemia were also considered but ruled out due to endemicity, long duration without further symptoms, and lack of localized oedema. Cutaneous leishmaniasis was considered the most likely diagnosis due to its frequency in the valley the patient had traveled to and the characteristic presentation (localized painless ulcer with raised edges).
management_and_clinical_course: Treatment was started with intravenous sodium stibogluconate (SSG, 20 mg/kg/day for 20 days), which is the first-line treatment for L. (V.) peruviana. Additionally, topical imiquimod therapy was administered every other day for 20 days. The response after 20 days of treatment was good (Fig. 2.2). At the third month of follow-up, the patient did not have any signs of relapse (Fig. 2.3).
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is cutaneous leishmaniasis, caused by Leishmania (Viannia) peruviana. This was confirmed by a positive leishmanin skin test and positive PCR results, in the context of a characteristic localized painless ulcer with raised edges on the nose and epidemiological exposure in an endemic area. The patient showed a good response to treatment with intravenous sodium stibogluconate and topical imiquimod therapy, with no relapse observed at 3 months follow-up.
